Abstract Background An inadequate protein intake may offset the muscle protein synthetic response after physical activity, reducing the possible benefits of an active lifestyle for muscle mass. We examined the effects of 12 weeks of daily protein supplementation on lean body mass, muscle strength, and physical performance in physically active older adults with a low habitual protein intake (<1.0 g/kg/day). Methods A randomized double‐blinded controlled trial was performed among 116 physically active older adults [age 69 (interquartile range: 67–73) years, 82% male] who were training for a 4 day walking event of 30, 40, or 50 km/day. Participants were randomly allocated to either 31 g of milk protein or iso‐caloric placebo supplementation for 12 weeks. Body composition (dual‐energy X‐ray absorptiometry), strength (isometric leg extension and grip strength), quadriceps contractile function, and physical performance [Short Physical Performance Battery, Timed Up‐and‐Go test, and cardiorespiratory fitness (Åstrand–Rhyming submaximal exercise test)] were measured at baseline and after 12 weeks. We assessed vitamin D status and markers of muscle damage and renal function in blood and urine samples before and after intervention. Results A larger increase in relative lean body mass was observed in the protein vs. placebo group (∆0.93 ± 1.22% vs. ∆0.44 ± 1.40%, P Interaction = 0.046). Absolute and relative fat mass decreased more in the protein group than in the placebo group (∆−0.90 ± 1.22 kg vs. ∆−0.31 ± 1.28 kg, P Interaction = 0.013 and ∆−0.92 ± 1.19% vs. ∆−0.39 ± 1.36%, P Interaction = 0.029, respectively). Strength and contractile function did not change in both groups. Gait speed, chair‐rise ability, Timed Up‐and‐Go, and cardiorespiratory fitness improved in both groups ( P < 0.001), but no between‐group differences were observed. Serum urea increased in the protein group, whereas no changes were observed in the placebo group ( P Interaction < 0.001). No between‐group differences were observed for vitamin D status, muscle damage, and renal function markers. Conclusions In physically active older adults with relatively low habitual dietary protein consumption, an improvement in physical performance, an increase in lean body mass, and a decrease in fat mass were observed after walking exercise training. A larger increase in relative lean body mass and larger reduction in fat mass were observed in participants receiving 12 weeks of daily protein supplementation compared with controls, whereas this was not accompanied by differences in improvements between groups in muscle strength and physical performance. Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle , 10 : 298 – 310 . 10.1002/jcsm.12394 . Introduction A physically active lifestyle attenuates the age‐related loss of muscle mass (i.e. sarcopenia) and associated decrements of muscle function 1 , 2 by increased muscle protein synthesis rates after exercise but also due to preservation of skeletal muscle sensitivity to dietary amino acids and suppressing the catabolic inflammatory cytokines in the muscle. 3 , 4 , 5 Sufficient protein intake is another vital component to maintain and regain muscle mass. 6 , 7 , 8 Current recommendations for adults advice 0.8 g/kg/day. 9 However, the PROT‐AGE study group suggested that older adults above 65 years of age should consume 1.0–1.2 g/kg/day to compensate for the attenuated capacity of protein utilization in the aging muscles. 6 For physically active older adults, their recommendation is even higher, i.e. ≥1.2 g/kg/day in order to comply with the synergistic effects of exercise and protein intake on muscle protein synthesis. 6 It has previously been shown that more than 50% of physically active older adults has a protein intake below 1.2 g/kg/day. 10 This observation suggests that physically active older adults may not consume enough protein to be utilized for the exercise‐induced improved muscle protein synthetic response and, thus, to prevent age‐related muscle mass loss. Therefore, we assessed the effects of 12 weeks of daily protein supplementation on lean body mass, muscle strength, and physical performance in physically active older adults with a low habitual protein intake. We hypothesized that protein supplementation in physically active older adults would induce beneficial effects on lean body mass, muscle strength, and physical performance, while no effects were expected in the control group receiving an iso‐caloric placebo.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Protein supplementation combined with walking exercise in physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Inadequate protein intake can impair muscle protein synthesis post-activity, making sufficient protein intake crucial to maintain and regain muscle mass, especially in aging muscles where utilization capacity is attenuated. Protein supplementation stimulates muscle protein synthesis, shifting protein balance to positive, thereby attenuating age-related muscle mass loss, leading to increased lean body mass and decreased fat mass. The resulting hypertrophy might be sarcoplasmic, rather than myofibrillar, which could explain the lack of direct strength improvement. Exercise acts as a primary stimulus for muscle synthesis, underscoring the critical role of adequate protein intake. An increase in serum urea indicates altered protein metabolism with supplementation.
related_biomarkers: skeletal muscle sensitivity to dietary amino acids

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The intervention involved 12 weeks of daily milk protein supplementation (MPC 80) vs. an iso-caloric placebo. The protein group received 31g of protein twice daily, totaling 62g protein/day, consumed during breakfast and within 30 minutes after exercise or during lunch on non-exercising days. This increased their daily protein intake from 0.86 ± 0.23 g/kg/day to 1.29 ± 0.28 g/kg/day, aligning with guidelines for physically active older adults. This dose led to a larger increase in lean body mass and a greater reduction in fat mass compared to the placebo group, with an observed increase in serum urea in the protein group.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The beneficial effects of protein supplementation were specific to body composition, leading to differential improvements in total body weight, whole-body lean mass (especially truncal lean body mass), total body fat mass, and fat mass/lean body mass ratio, with these effects being more pronounced in women. An increase in serum urea was also specific to the protein group. However, no between-group differences were observed for muscle strength, contractile function, physical performance measures (gait speed, chair-rise ability, Timed Up-and-Go, cardiorespiratory fitness/estimated VO2max), vitamin D status, muscle damage markers, or other renal function markers (creatinine, eGFR, urinary albumin/creatinine ratio). Improvements in physical performance and certain biochemical measures in both groups were primarily attributed to walking exercise training rather than protein supplementation alone, suggesting a potential ceiling effect for physical performance improvements in already highly active individuals.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: The target population consisted of 116 generally healthy, physically active older adults (men and women at least 65 years old; age 69, 82% male, predominantly Caucasian) with a habitual protein intake below 1.0 g/kg/day. They were registered and training for the 2017 Nijmegen Four Days Marches (30, 40, or 50 km/day). Exclusion criteria included type 1 or 2 diabetes, milk protein allergy/lactose intolerance, COPD, cancer, renal insufficiency (eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m-1), intestinal diseases affecting protein uptake, statin use, or involvement in heavy resistance exercise programs.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Protein supplementation in physically active older adults with low habitual dietary protein intake, when combined with exercise, effectively improves body composition by increasing lean body mass and decreasing fat mass. This can delay age-related loss of muscle mass (sarcopenia), potentially saving 1–2 years of muscle decline, which is critical for long-term daily life mobility and physical resilience. Specifically, improved truncal body composition is linked to reduced risks for cardiovascular diseases, metabolic syndrome, improved postural stability, and reduced fall risk. Overall, it is an effective and safe strategy to attenuate age-related muscle loss and enhance the health benefits of an active lifestyle.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Protective benefit and health improvement for muscle mass maintenance and fat mass reduction. The intervention is classified as a safe strategy. While an increase in serum urea was observed in the protein group, it was not accompanied by changes in other renal function markers, suggesting it was not considered an adverse risk in this context.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), Timed Up-and-Go (TUG), and the Short Questionnaire to Assess Health-enhancing physical activity are considered reliable and valid methods in older adults. Repeated 24-hour recall is a validated method for assessing protein intake. However, physical performance measurements like SPPB and TUG were likely not sensitive enough to detect improvements in already high-functioning participants, suggesting a potential ceiling effect. The document notes that while 24h urine creatinine is the gold standard for renal function, it was not collected, although eGFR and urinary albumin/creatinine ratio indicated unaffected renal function. No explicit assessment of the reliability (sensitivity/specificity) for all measured biomarkers (e.g., DXA for body composition) was provided, but significant changes were reported for lean body mass, fat mass, and serum urea.
